```{python}
#| include: false
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns
from data2thesis import load_case_study

navy = "#1d588c"
copper = "#b4762e"
soft = "#46586d"

sns.set_theme(style="whitegrid", font_scale=1.1)
plt.rcParams["figure.figsize"] = (6, 4)
plt.rcParams["figure.dpi"] = 150
plt.rcParams["axes.edgecolor"] = "#cccccc"
plt.rcParams["axes.linewidth"] = 0.8

students = load_case_study("students")
semesters = load_case_study("semesters")

first_sem = semesters[semesters["semester"] == 1].merge(students, on="student_id")

wellbeing_by_sem = (
    semesters.merge(students[["student_id", "workshop"]], on="student_id")
    .groupby(["semester", "workshop"], as_index=False)["wellbeing"]
    .mean()
)

faculty_means = (
    first_sem.groupby("faculty", as_index=False)["wellbeing"]
    .mean()
    .sort_values("wellbeing")
)

anscombe = sns.load_dataset("anscombe")
```

# Data Visualization

A graph is an instrument and an argument

**Chapter 4**

Polla Fattah

---

## By the end of today you can

- explain why graphs are needed alongside numerical summaries;
- tell exploratory graphs from explanatory ones;
- explain why position and length are read more accurately than angle, area, or colour;
- choose a graph from the question and the variables;
- build graphs with Seaborn and Matplotlib from data, visual mappings, and axes;
- judge whether a graph is honest, and improve a misleading one;
- export figures at the size and resolution a thesis needs.

---

## Summaries can hide almost anything

```python
anscombe.groupby("dataset").agg(
    mean_x=("x", "mean"),
    mean_y=("y", "mean"),
    std_y=("y", "std")
)
```

| Dataset | mean x | mean y | std y | correlation |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| I to IV | 9.0 | 7.5 | 2.03 | 0.82 |

Anscombe's four datasets share every numerical summary.

---

## Four identical summaries, four different stories

```{python}
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 3.2
g = sns.lmplot(
    data=anscombe,
    x="x",
    y="y",
    col="dataset",
    ci=None,
    height=3.0,
    aspect=0.8,
    scatter_kws={"s": 40, "color": navy},
    line_kws={"color": copper, "linewidth": 2}
)
g.set_axis_labels("x", "y")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

A line, a curve, an outlier, and one point making the whole trend.

---

## Look first

> **Anyone who analysed these data without looking would draw the same, wrong, conclusion from all four.**

Many errors in data, and in reasoning about data, are found only by looking.

---

## Exploring and explaining

| | Exploratory graph | Explanatory graph |
|---|---|---|
| for | the researcher | the reader |
| purpose | understand the data | show a known finding |
| number | many, quickly | a few, carefully |
| polish | none needed | clear message and labels |

A thesis contains a few explanatory graphs, chosen from many exploratory ones.

---

## A graph turns numbers into visual properties

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    A["Position on a<br>common scale"] --> B["Length"] --> C["Angle<br>and slope"] --> D["Area"] --> E["Colour<br>shade"]
```

Cleveland and McGill's experiments: judged most accurately on the left, least on the right.

Put the most important comparison into position or length.

---

## The same five numbers, two ways

```{python}
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 3.6
shares = pd.DataFrame({
    "group": ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E"],
    "percent": [23, 21, 20, 19, 17]
})

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 3.6))

# Pie chart
colors = sns.color_palette("mako", n_colors=5)
axes[0].pie(shares["percent"], labels=shares["group"], colors=colors, startangle=90)
axes[0].set_title("Pie: Differences hard to discern")

# Bar chart
sns.barplot(data=shares, x="group", y="percent", color=navy, ax=axes[1])
axes[1].set_ylabel("Percent (%)")
axes[1].set_xlabel(None)
axes[1].set_title("Bar: Decline from A to E is obvious")

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

In the pie the slices look equal. In the bars the decline from A to E is obvious.

---

## Two more rules of thumb

- put values to be compared **next to each other on the same scale**, within one panel;
- use colour to **separate a few categories**, not to carry the main message.

Prefer bar charts and dot plots to pie charts, and scatter plots to bubble charts.

---

## Choosing a graph

| Question | Variables | Graph | Seaborn tool |
|---|---|---|---|
| how are values distributed? | one numeric | histogram, KDE | `sns.histplot`, `sns.kdeplot` |
| how many in each category? | one categorical | count bar chart | `sns.countplot` |
| do groups differ? | numeric by categorical | box plot, strip plot | `sns.boxplot`, `sns.stripplot` |
| how are two variables related? | two numeric | scatter, regression | `sns.scatterplot`, `sns.regplot` |
| how does it change over time? | numeric over time | line chart | `sns.lineplot` |
| how do many variables relate? | several numeric | heat map | `sns.heatmap` |

---

## The anatomy of Python visualization

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    D["Data<br>Pandas DataFrame"] --> S["Seaborn<br>Statistical abstraction"] --> M["Matplotlib<br>Axes & Figure control"]
```

Seaborn creates statistical graphics with one concise call, while Matplotlib lets you customize titles, limits, and annotations.

## Figure and Axes give the canvas

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column}
```python
pilot = pd.DataFrame({
    "sleep": [6.5, 7.5, 5.5, 8.0, 6.0],
    "stress": [3.2, 2.1, 4.5, 1.8, 3.9]
})

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 3.5))
ax.set_xlabel("Sleep (hours)")
ax.set_ylabel("Stress (1 to 5)")
plt.show()
```

The axes exist, but nothing is drawn yet.
:::
::: {.column}
```{python}
#| fig-width: 4.3
#| fig-height: 3.4
pilot = pd.DataFrame({
    "sleep": [6.5, 7.5, 5.5, 8.0, 6.0],
    "stress": [3.2, 2.1, 4.5, 1.8, 3.9]
})
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4.3, 3.4))
ax.set_xlabel("Sleep (hours)")
ax.set_ylabel("Stress (1 to 5)")
ax.set_xlim(5, 9)
ax.set_ylim(1, 5)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```
:::
::::

## Seaborn draws the data onto the axes

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column}
```python
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 3.5))
sns.scatterplot(
    data=pilot,
    x="sleep",
    y="stress",
    s=80,
    color="#1d588c",
    ax=ax
)
plt.show()
```

One point per row. Passing `ax=ax` connects Seaborn directly to the Matplotlib canvas.
:::
::: {.column}
```{python}
#| fig-width: 4.3
#| fig-height: 3.4
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4.3, 3.4))
sns.scatterplot(data=pilot, x="sleep", y="stress", s=80, color=navy, ax=ax)
ax.set_xlabel("Sleep (hours)")
ax.set_ylabel("Stress (1 to 5)")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```
:::
::::

## One row per student

```python
first_sem = (
    semesters[semesters["semester"] == 1]
    .merge(students, on="student_id")
)
```

Each student's first-semester record, with their background information.

Most graphs are simplest with one row per case.

## Histograms show a distribution

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column}
```python
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 3.5))
sns.histplot(
    data=first_sem,
    x="sleep_hours",
    binwidth=0.5,
    color="steelblue",
    edgecolor="white",
    ax=ax
)
```

Bell-shaped, centred a little above 6 hours.

`r round(100 * (first_sem['sleep_hours'] < 7).mean())`% of students sleep less than the recommended 7.
:::
::: {.column}
```{python}
#| fig-width: 4.3
#| fig-height: 3.4
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4.3, 3.4))
sns.histplot(data=first_sem, x="sleep_hours", binwidth=0.5, color=navy, edgecolor="white", ax=ax)
ax.set_xlabel("Hours of Sleep per Night")
ax.set_ylabel("Student Count")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```
:::
::::

---

## The binwidth changes the picture

```{python}
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 3.2
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(9, 3.2))
for ax, bw in zip(axes, [0.1, 0.5, 2.0]):
    sns.histplot(data=first_sem, x="sleep_hours", binwidth=bw, color=navy, edgecolor="white", ax=ax)
    ax.set_title(f"binwidth = {bw}")
    ax.set_xlabel("Sleep (hours)")
    ax.set_ylabel(None)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Too narrow is noisy, too wide hides the shape. Try a few widths.

## Count charts count categories

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column}
```python
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 3.5))
sns.countplot(
    data=students,
    y="faculty",

```

`sns.countplot()` counts rows automatically.

For precomputed values such as averages, use `sns.barplot()`.
:::
::: {.column}

```{python}
#| fig-height: 3.4
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4.3, 3.4))
sns.countplot(data=students, y="faculty", color=navy, ax=ax)
ax.set_xlabel("Number of Students")
ax.set_ylabel(None)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

```{python}
#| fig-width: 4.3

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4.3, 3.4))
sns.boxplot(data=first_sem, x="study_mode", y="wellbeing", color="#eaf0f7", ax=ax)
```

::::

---

## Reading a box plot

| Part | Shows |
|---|---|
| box | the interquartile range (IQR, middle 50%) |
| line inside | the median |
| whiskers | typical range ($1.5 \times \text{IQR}$) |
| points beyond | outliers / extreme values |

Whether the study-mode difference is larger than chance is a question for Chapter 8.

---

## Scatter plots show relationships

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column}
```python
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 3.5))
sns.regplot(
    data=first_sem,
    x="sleep_hours",
    y="gpa",
    scatter_kws={"alpha": 0.35, "color": "#1d588c"},
    line_kws={"color": "#b4762e"},
    ax=ax
)
```

`alpha` makes points transparent against **overplotting**.

The line rises gently, but points scatter widely.
:::
::: {.column}
```{python}
#| fig-width: 4.3
#| fig-height: 3.4
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4.3, 3.4))
sns.regplot(
    data=first_sem,
    x="sleep_hours",
    y="gpa",
    scatter_kws={"alpha": 0.35, "color": navy},
    line_kws={"color": copper},
    ax=ax
)
ax.set_xlabel("Hours of Sleep per Night")
ax.set_ylabel("Grade Point Average (0 to 4)")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```
:::
::::

## Line charts show change over time

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column}
```python
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 3.5))
sns.lineplot(
    data=wellbeing_by_sem,
    x="semester",
    y="wellbeing",
    hue="workshop",
    marker="o",
    palette=["#1d588c", "#b4762e"],
    ax=ax
)
```

Shows the longitudinal trajectory across all four study periods.
:::
::: {.column}
```{python}
#| fig-width: 4.3
#| fig-height: 3.4
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4.3, 3.4))
sns.lineplot(
    data=wellbeing_by_sem,
    x="semester",
    y="wellbeing",
    hue="workshop",
    marker="o",
    palette=[navy, copper],
    ax=ax
)
ax.set_xticks([1, 2, 3, 4])
ax.set_xlabel("Semester")
ax.set_ylabel("Average Wellbeing (0 to 100)")
ax.legend(title="Workshop", loc="lower right", frameon=True)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```
:::
::::

---

## Mapping (`hue`) vs Setting (`color`)

```python
sns.lineplot(data=df, x="x", y="y", hue="group")   # mapped: color varies by group
sns.histplot(data=df, x="x", color="steelblue")   # set: one fixed color everywhere
```

| | Data Mapping (`hue`) | Fixed Styling (`color`) |
|---|---|---|
| meaning | depends on variable values | uniform for the entire plot |
| legend | created automatically | no redundant legend |

---

## A common visualization mistake

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column}
```python
# Unnecessary mapping for one constant
sns.barplot(
    data=faculty_means,
    x="faculty",
    y="wellbeing",
    hue="faculty"  # redundant!
)
```

Using `hue` for categorical variables already labeled on the axis creates visual clutter and a useless legend.
:::
::: {.column}
```{python}
#| fig-width: 4.3
#| fig-height: 3.4
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4.3, 3.4))
sns.barplot(data=faculty_means, x="faculty", y="wellbeing", hue="faculty", ax=ax)
ax.set_ylim(0, 100)
ax.set_xlabel(None)
ax.set_ylabel("Wellbeing")
ax.tick_params(axis="x", rotation=30)
ax.legend(bbox_to_anchor=(1.02, 1), loc="upper left", borderaxespad=0)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```
:::
::::

---

## From exploratory to explanatory

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    A["Descriptive Labels"] --> B["Honest Scales"] --> C["Accessible Palettes"] --> D["Targeted Annotations"]
```

Each addition is a purposeful design decision to aid reader comprehension.

---

## Clear labels with measurement units

```python
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))
sns.lineplot(
    data=wellbeing_by_sem,
    x="semester",
    y="wellbeing",
    hue="workshop",
    marker="o",
    ax=ax
)
ax.set_title("Student Wellbeing Trajectory Over Two Years", fontsize=13, weight="bold")
ax.set_xlabel("Semester (Measurement Wave)", fontsize=11)
ax.set_ylabel("Mean Wellbeing Score (0 to 100)", fontsize=11)
```

Always include the scale range or physical units in parentheses.

---

## Colour-blind-friendly palettes

- **Qualitative**: `palette="tab10"` or `palette="Set2"` for unordered groups.
- **Sequential**: `palette="viridis"` or `palette="Blues"` for numeric quantities.
- **Diverging**: `palette="vlag"` or `palette="coolwarm"` centered on a neutral midpoint.

Roughly 8% of men and 0.5% of women have color vision deficiency; avoid rainbow/jet palettes.

---

## Annotations give immediate reference

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column}
```python
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 3.5))
sns.histplot(data=first_sem, x="sleep_hours", binwidth=0.5, ax=ax)

ax.axvline(7, color="darkred", linestyle="--")
ax.text(7.1, 75, "Recommended: 7h", color="darkred")
```

Guides the eye directly to the clinical or theoretical threshold.
:::
::: {.column}
```{python}
#| fig-width: 4.3
#| fig-height: 3.4
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4.3, 3.4))
sns.histplot(data=first_sem, x="sleep_hours", binwidth=0.5, color=navy, edgecolor="white", ax=ax)
ax.axvline(7, color=copper, linestyle="--", linewidth=1.5)
ax.text(7.1, 65, "Recommended:\n7 hours", color=copper, fontsize=10, weight="bold")
ax.set_xlabel("Hours of Sleep per Night")
ax.set_ylabel("Student Count")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```
:::
::::

## A graph can be accurate and still mislead

Most misleading graphs are not deliberate fraud—they arise from unexamined software defaults.

| Design Choice | Research Risk |
|---|---|
| Truncated bar axis | Bar lengths exaggerate minute group differences |
| Squashed aspect ratio | Artificially steepens or flattens trends |
| 3D effects / Clutter | Distorts perspective and distracts from data |
| Rainbow palettes | False boundaries created by perceptual non-uniformity |

---

## Bar axes must start at zero

A bar represents quantity through **physical length** from the baseline.

If the axis is truncated, a bar twice as tall no longer indicates twice as much value.

Points, lines, and dot plots represent quantity through **position**, allowing zoomed views if clearly noted in the caption.

---

## A misleading graph: truncated baseline

```{python}
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 3.4
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 3.4))
sns.barplot(data=faculty_means, x="faculty", y="wellbeing", color="crimson", ax=ax)
ax.set_ylim(58, 62.5)
ax.set_title("MISLEADING: Truncated axis at 58 exaggerates a 3-point difference")
ax.set_ylabel("Wellbeing (58 to 62.5)")
ax.set_xlabel(None)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Education appears several times taller than Social Sciences, yet actual averages differ by only 3 points out of 100!

---

## The same data, redesigned honestly

```{python}
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 3.4
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 3.4))
sns.stripplot(
    data=first_sem,
    x="wellbeing",
    y="faculty",
    order=faculty_means["faculty"],
    alpha=0.25,
    color="grey",
    jitter=0.2,
    ax=ax
)
sns.pointplot(
    data=first_sem,
    x="wellbeing",
    y="faculty",
    order=faculty_means["faculty"],
    color=copper,
    markers="D",
    linestyles="none",
    errorbar=None,
    ax=ax
)
ax.set_xlabel("Wellbeing in Semester 1 (0 to 100)")
ax.set_ylabel(None)
ax.set_title("REDESIGNED: Individual points reveal that within-faculty variance dwarfs group differences")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Differences between faculties are negligible compared to the substantial variation among individual students.

---

## Facets: small multiples

:::: {.columns}

```python
g = sns.FacetGrid(
    first_sem,
    col="programme",

g.map_dataframe(
```

```{python}
g.map_dataframe(sns.scatterplot, x="sleep_hours", y="gpa", alpha=0.35, color=navy, s=20)
g.set_axis_labels("Sleep (h)", "GPA")

plt.show()
```

## Density plots compare whole distributions

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column}
```python
sem2 = (
    semesters[semesters["semester"] == 2]
    .merge(students, on="student_id")
)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 3.5))
sns.kdeplot(
    data=sem2,
    x="wellbeing",
    hue="workshop",
    fill=True,
    alpha=0.3,
    palette=[navy, copper],
    ax=ax
)
```

Shows that the entire distribution shifted upward, not just a handful of students.
:::
::: {.column}
```{python}
#| fig-width: 4.3
#| fig-height: 3.4
sem2 = semesters[semesters["semester"] == 2].merge(students, on="student_id")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4.3, 3.4))
sns.kdeplot(data=sem2, x="wellbeing", hue="workshop", fill=True, alpha=0.35, palette=[navy, copper], ax=ax)
ax.set_xlabel("Wellbeing Score (0 to 100)")
ax.set_ylabel("Kernel Density")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```
:::
::::

---

## Correlation heatmaps

```{python}
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 4.0
corr_vars = ["gpa", "sleep_hours", "study_hours", "wellbeing", "caffeine_mg"]
corr = first_sem[corr_vars].corr()

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 4.0))
sns.heatmap(
    corr,
    annot=True,
    fmt=".2f",
    cmap="vlag",
    vmin=-1,
    vmax=1,
    center=0,
    square=True,
    linewidths=0.5,
    cbar_kws={"label": "Pearson r"},
    ax=ax
)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

A diverging palette centered at 0 with overlaid numeric coefficients prevents misreading subtle color tints.

---

## Exporting publication-ready figures

```python
# High-resolution raster for thesis drafts
fig.savefig("figures/wellbeing.png", dpi=300, bbox_inches="tight")

# Scalable vector graphics for final submission
fig.savefig("figures/wellbeing.pdf", bbox_inches="tight")
```

| Decision | Recommended Practice |
|---|---|
| Width | 8 cm (single-column) or 16 cm (full page width) |
| Resolution | At least 300 DPI for raster formats |
| Format | PDF or SVG for publication; PNG for web / slides |
| Font size | Minimum 9–10 pt when rendered at final physical dimensions |

## Completion checklist

- [ ] Every variable was visually inspected prior to formal inferential testing;
- [ ] Plot type matches the research question and variable measurement levels;
- [ ] The primary comparison is encoded using position or length;
- [ ] Axes include descriptive variable titles and measurement units;
- [ ] Bar charts strictly start at zero baseline;
- [ ] Color palettes are accessible, color-blind friendly, and non-redundant;
- [ ] Visualizations are saved at reproduction dimensions with `bbox_inches="tight"`.

---

## The chapter in one sentence

> **Inspect the distribution of your data first, then choose a visualization that encodes key comparisons into position or length while honestly conveying magnitude.**

## Questions & Discussion

Think of a published graph that influenced your thinking.

Would its conclusion remain compelling if the vertical axis were reset to its theoretical baseline?
